description: Proving Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2022.

talks.title: How to Succeed as a Freelance Pentester
talks.teaser: Covers the readiness, business setup, insurance, and client-finding steps needed to run a freelance penetration testing practice.
talks.summary:
The talk is aimed at penetration testers considering leaving employment to work freelance. The speaker starts with the personal question of why someone wants to freelance. Setting your own hours and choosing clients comes with uneven workloads and the need to find all of your own work. He suggests listing the testing areas you can sell, such as web applications or external testing, and checking whether you can draw out a client's goals and data concerns.

The middle section covers setup costs and protections. He recommends forming a legal entity so personal assets are shielded from client claims, and carrying general liability, errors and omissions, and professional liability insurance. A business lawyer should review client agreements; he gives an example of keeping ownership of his own scripts after a contract review. An accountant who understands self-employment taxes and quarterly payments is also worth the fee. He estimates total startup costs at roughly five to ten thousand dollars.

For finding work, he compares subcontracting through consultancies, which is easier to start but pays less, with direct clients, which pays more but demands sales and proposal work. To set a rate, he works backward from a target salary and doubles the hourly figure to cover unbillable time. He credits networking and conference contacts as a strong source of leads, and says testimonials help a solo operator, who has no company brand to hide behind.

talks.title: Oauth third party not departing
talks.teaser: Shows how OAuth consent and device code flows let attackers keep SaaS access after an admin disables the app.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how OAuth 2 holds up in SaaS environments. It starts with the consent flow, which hands an application a token that keeps working without asking the user again. The speakers note that the original editor of the standard withdrew his name over concerns about complexity, and they recall a 2018 Google Docs worm that abused app scripts to phish contacts. They then describe how Microsoft and Google responded with publisher verification and admin consent requirements for newly registered apps.

The middle section covers attack paths that still work around those controls. Device code flow is the main example: an attacker starts the flow, phishes a victim into entering a code on a legitimate login page, and receives tokens without a client secret or a consent prompt, which can also get past multi-factor checks. The speakers also list persistence options after a compromise, such as adding credentials to an application, changing recovery details, and using legacy protocols that do not enforce MFA.

The closing part presents a watchdog technique. A script uses the Microsoft Graph API and a refresh token to re-enable an app that an administrator has disabled, so access continues quietly. The talk argues that disabling a suspicious app is better practice than deleting it, and it closes with a short section on solutions.

talks.title: Reverse engineering a DOS PC FMV Game from 1994
talks.teaser: Walks through reverse engineering a 1994 DOS full-motion video game, from its file formats to its hidden switches.
talks.summary:
The talk examines The Lawnmower Man, a 1994 DOS game built around full-motion video, and asks how a PC release of it could run at all. The speaker starts with the play experience: quick-time sequences, timed logic puzzles, a five-second pause that restarts the game, and a memory setup that made it hard to run on period machines. The focus then moves to the CD contents. Files with sound-like names turn out to be Amiga-era formats, including sound modules, Deluxe Paint animations, and a path map that hard-codes install locations, so renaming the directory breaks the game. The playback executable's case-sensitive command switches are documented, and a batch-based level selector is demonstrated.

The investigation links the game to the Commodore CD TV, a console discontinued during its development, and to the Amiga more broadly. The speaker proposes that the video files are raw footage in a Video Toaster-style format, and that the game likely played two video streams at once from a single-speed drive. An account from a developer supports the idea that the game was originally an Amiga title. The audience also attempts a logic puzzle live, which shows how unforgiving the design was.

The takeaway is practical: old media formats and undocumented install logic can be recovered with period-appropriate tools and patient file inspection. Full decoding of the video was still in progress at the time of the talk, and the speaker invited the community to help finish it.
